subject.name: Mathematics
subject.overview: ICSE Class 9 Mathematics builds the base for the Class 10 board course. In arithmetic and algebra it covers rational and irrational numbers, compound interest, expansions, factorisation, simultaneous linear equations, indices and logarithms. Geometry is proof-based: congruent and isosceles triangles, the mid-point theorem, Pythagoras theorem, properties of polygons and quadrilaterals, and chord properties of circles. The course also introduces statistics (frequency tables, mean and median), mensuration of plane figures and cuboids, trigonometric ratios of acute and standard angles, and co-ordinate geometry including graphs and the distance formula. Students are expected to show clear working and give reasons for each step in proofs.
studyTips: Write out the key identities (squares, cubes, laws of indices and logarithms) on one sheet and practise using them in reverse, since factorisation is expansion run backwards.
In geometry proofs, state a reason in brackets beside every step (given, common, SAS, angles opposite equal sides) exactly as you would in an exam answer.
For compound interest and mensuration, write the formula first, substitute with units, and check whether the answer is reasonable before moving on.
After solving an equation, substitute the answer back into the original equation; for logarithm equations also reject any root that makes a log argument non-positive.
Memorise the table of trigonometric ratios for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and draw a labelled right triangle before writing any ratio.

chapters.name: Rational and Irrational Numbers
chapters.summary: Classifies real numbers as rational or irrational and develops the simplification of surds, including rationalising denominators.

chapters.name: Compound Interest
chapters.summary: Computes compound interest year by year and by formula, and applies the same idea to growth and depreciation.

chapters.name: Expansions
chapters.summary: Uses standard algebraic identities to expand squares and cubes of binomials and to evaluate related expressions.

topics.name: Square of a binomial and trinomial

chapters.name: Factorisation
chapters.summary: Factorises expressions by taking common factors, grouping, splitting the middle term and using the difference of squares and sum or difference of cubes.

topics.name: Difference of squares, sum and difference of cubes

chapters.name: Simultaneous Linear Equations
chapters.summary: Solves pairs of linear equations in two variables algebraically and applies them to word problems.

chapters.name: Indices
chapters.summary: Applies the laws of indices to simplify expressions with integral and fractional exponents and to solve exponential equations.

chapters.name: Logarithms
chapters.summary: Relates logarithmic and exponential forms and uses the laws of logarithms to evaluate and solve equations.

chapters.name: Triangles (Congruency)
chapters.summary: Establishes the congruence criteria for triangles and uses them to prove equality of sides and angles.

chapters.name: Isosceles Triangles
chapters.summary: Uses the theorem that angles opposite equal sides are equal, and its converse, to find angles and write proofs.

chapters.name: Mid-point Theorem
chapters.summary: Studies the mid-point theorem, its converse and the equal intercept theorem, with applications to triangles and quadrilaterals.

chapters.name: Pythagoras Theorem
chapters.summary: Proves and applies Pythagoras theorem and its converse to right-angled triangles.

chapters.name: Rectilinear Figures
chapters.summary: Covers angle sums of polygons, regular polygons and the properties of quadrilaterals such as parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses and squares.

chapters.name: Circle
chapters.summary: Develops chord properties of circles, including the perpendicular from the centre and equal chords.

topics.name: Perpendicular from the centre to a chord

chapters.name: Statistics
chapters.summary: Organises data into frequency distributions and computes the mean and median of ungrouped data.

chapters.name: Mensuration
chapters.summary: Finds areas and perimeters of plane figures, including triangles by Heron’s formula, and surface areas and volumes of cubes and cuboids.

topics.name: Area and perimeter of plane figures
Area of a triangle by Heron’s formula
Surface area and volume of cubes and cuboids

chapters.name: Trigonometry
chapters.summary: Defines trigonometric ratios for acute angles, evaluates them for standard angles and uses complementary-angle relations.

chapters.name: Co-ordinate Geometry
chapters.summary: Locates points in the Cartesian plane, draws graphs of linear equations and applies the distance formula.

questions.text: Which of the following is an irrational number?
questions.explanation: √12 = 2√3 and √3 is irrational; √49 = 7, 0.375 = 3/8 and 22/7 are all rational.

questions.text: If x = 1/(3 − 2√2), find the value of x + 1/x.
questions.explanation: Rationalise first; the surd parts cancel when x and 1/x are added.
Uses (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².

questions.explanation: For depreciation the rate is subtracted inside the bracket.

(a) Find the sum.
(b) Find the compound interest for the third year.
questions.explanation: Interest for a particular year is the rate applied to the amount at the start of that year.

questions.text: If a + b = 7 and ab = 10, then a² + b² equals:
If x + 1/x = 4, find the value of x³ + 1/x³.

questions.explanation: −2 and −3 multiply to 6 and add to −5.

questions.text: Factorise completely: a³ − 27b³.
questions.explanation: Uses x³ − y³ = (x − y)(x² + xy + y²).

questions.text: Factorise 6x² + 7x − 3 by splitting the middle term.
questions.answer:
Product of first and last coefficients = 6 × (−3) = −18. Two numbers with product −18 and sum 7 are 9 and −2.
6x² + 9x − 2x − 3 = 3x(2x + 3) − 1(2x + 3) = (2x + 3)(3x − 1).

questions.text: The sum of two numbers is 50 and their difference is 14. Find the larger number.
questions.answer:
Let the numbers be x and y (x > y).
x + y = 50, x − y = 14.
Adding: 2x = 64, so x = 32 (and y = 18).
The larger number is 32.

questions.text: A fraction becomes 1/2 when 1 is added to both its numerator and denominator. It becomes 1/3 when 1 is subtracted from both. Find the fraction.
questions.answer:
Let the fraction be x/y.
(x + 1)/(y + 1) = 1/2 ⇒ 2x + 2 = y + 1 ⇒ y = 2x + 1 … (i)
(x − 1)/(y − 1) = 1/3 ⇒ 3x − 3 = y − 1 ⇒ y = 3x − 2 … (ii)
From (i) and (ii): 2x + 1 = 3x − 2 ⇒ x = 3, y = 7.
The fraction is 3/7. (Check: 4/8 = 1/2 and 2/6 = 1/3.)

questions.text: The value of 16^(3/4) is:
Solve for x: 2^(x + 3) = 32^(x − 1).
questions.explanation: Write both sides with the same base, then equate the powers.

questions.text: The value of log₂ 64 is:
questions.explanation: Since 2⁶ = 64.

questions.text: Evaluate (logarithms to base 10): log 25 + log 8 − log 2.
questions.answer: log 25 + log 8 − log 2 = log(25 × 8 ÷ 2) = log 100 = log 10² = 2.

questions.text: Solve for x (logarithms to base 10): log x + log (x − 3) = 1.
questions.answer:
log[x(x − 3)] = 1 = log 10 ⇒ x(x − 3) = 10 ⇒ x² − 3x − 10 = 0 ⇒ (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0 ⇒ x = 5 or x = −2.
Logarithms are defined only for positive numbers, so x and x − 3 must be positive; x = −2 is rejected.
Hence x = 5.
questions.explanation: Always check roots against the condition that the argument of a log is positive.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a valid criterion for congruence of triangles?
questions.answer: SSA is not a valid criterion.
questions.explanation: Two sides and a non-included angle do not fix a triangle uniquely.

questions.text: In quadrilateral ABCD, AB = AD and diagonal AC bisects ∠BAD. Prove that △ABC ≅ △ADC and hence that BC = DC.
questions.answer:
In △ABC and △ADC:
AB = AD (given)
∠BAC = ∠DAC (AC bisects ∠BAD)
AC = AC (common)
So △ABC ≅ △ADC (SAS).
Hence BC = DC (corresponding parts of congruent triangles).

questions.text: In △ABC, AB = AC and ∠A = 40°. Find ∠B.
In △ABC, AB = AC. Side BA is produced to D such that AD = AB. Prove that ∠BCD = 90°.
questions.answer:
AB = AC ⇒ ∠ABC = ∠ACB = x (say).
AD = AB = AC ⇒ in △ACD, ∠ACD = ∠ADC = y (say).
In △BCD: ∠DBC + ∠BDC + ∠BCD = 180°
⇒ x + y + (x + y) = 180° (since ∠BCD = ∠ACB + ∠ACD = x + y)
⇒ 2(x + y) = 180° ⇒ x + y = 90°.
Hence ∠BCD = 90°.
questions.explanation: Angles opposite equal sides are equal; apply this in both small triangles.

questions.text: The line segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and equal to ____ of it.
D, E and F are the mid-points of sides AB, BC and CA of △ABC. If AB = 8 cm, BC = 10 cm and CA = 12 cm, find the perimeter of △DEF.
questions.answer:
By the mid-point theorem, DE = CA/2 = 6 cm, EF = AB/2 = 4 cm, DF = BC/2 = 5 cm.
Perimeter of △DEF = 6 + 4 + 5 = 15 cm.
questions.explanation: The perimeter of the mid-point triangle is half the perimeter of the original triangle.

questions.text: A 13 m long ladder leans against a wall and reaches a window 12 m above the ground. How far is the foot of the ladder from the wall?

In △ABC, ∠B = 90° and D is the mid-point of BC.
(a) Prove that 4AD² = 4AB² + BC².
(b) If AB = 6 cm and BC = 16 cm, find AD.
questions.answer:
(a) In right △ABD, ∠B = 90°, so AD² = AB² + BD². Since D is the mid-point of BC, BD = BC/2.
AD² = AB² + BC²/4 ⇒ 4AD² = 4AB² + BC².
(b) 4AD² = 4 × 36 + 256 = 144 + 256 = 400 ⇒ AD² = 100 ⇒ AD = 10 cm.

questions.text: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. Find the number of sides.
questions.answer:
Each exterior angle = 180° − 150° = 30°.
Number of sides = 360° ÷ 30° = 12.

questions.text: The sum of the interior angles of a hexagon is:
In parallelogram ABCD, the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Prove that ∠APB = 90°.
questions.answer:
In a parallelogram, adjacent angles are supplementary: ∠A + ∠B = 180° (AD ∥ BC, co-interior angles).
So ½∠A + ½∠B = 90°, i.e. ∠PAB + ∠PBA = 90°.
In △APB: ∠APB = 180° − (∠PAB + ∠PBA) = 180° − 90° = 90°.

questions.text: A chord of length 16 cm is at a distance of 6 cm from the centre of a circle. Find the radius of the circle.
questions.answer:
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so half-chord = 8 cm.
r² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100 ⇒ r = 10 cm.

questions.text: The perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord ____ the chord.
questions.answer: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.

questions.text: Two parallel chords AB and CD of a circle of radius 13 cm have lengths 10 cm and 24 cm respectively. If the chords lie on opposite sides of the centre, find the distance between them.
questions.answer:
Distance of AB from centre = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm.
Distance of CD from centre = √(13² − 12²) = √(169 − 144) = √25 = 5 cm.
Chords on opposite sides ⇒ distance between them = 12 + 5 = 17 cm.
questions.explanation: If the chords were on the same side, the distance would be 12 − 5 = 7 cm.

questions.text:
The marks of 8 students are: 12, 15, 9, 20, 14, 18, 11, 13.
(a) Find the mean.
(b) Find the median.
(c) If a ninth student scoring 25 is included, find the new median.
The class mark of the class interval 20–30 is:
Find the area of a triangle whose sides are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.
Find the total surface area of a cuboid of length 10 cm, breadth 8 cm and height 5 cm.

A cuboidal water tank, open at the top, measures 3 m long, 2 m wide and 1.5 m deep.
(a) Find its capacity in litres.
(b) Find the area of metal sheet needed to make it.
(c) Find the cost of the sheet at ₹150 per m².
questions.answer:
(a) Volume = 3 × 2 × 1.5 = 9 m³. Since 1 m³ = 1000 litres, capacity = 9000 litres.
(b) Area = base + four walls = lb + 2h(l + b) = 3 × 2 + 2 × 1.5 × (3 + 2) = 6 + 15 = 21 m².
(c) Cost = 21 × 150 = ₹3150.
questions.explanation: An open tank has no top face, so only one l × b face is counted.

questions.text: If θ is acute and sin θ = 3/5, then cos θ equals:
questions.explanation: Taking opposite = 3 and hypotenuse = 5, adjacent = √(25 − 9) = 4, so cos θ = 4/5.

questions.text: Evaluate: sin² 60° + cos² 30° − tan² 45°.
Without using tables, evaluate: sin 35°/cos 55° + tan 20° × tan 70°.

In △ABC, ∠B = 90°, AB = 5 cm and AC = 13 cm.
(a) Find BC.
(b) Write sin A, cos A and tan A.
(c) Verify that sin² A + cos² A = 1.
(d) Find the value of tan A − cot C.
questions.answer:
(a) BC = √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12 cm.
(b) sin A = BC/AC = 12/13, cos A = AB/AC = 5/13, tan A = BC/AB = 12/5.
(c) sin² A + cos² A = 144/169 + 25/169 = 169/169 = 1. Verified.
(d) cot C = (side adjacent to C)/(side opposite C) = BC/AB = 12/5. So tan A − cot C = 12/5 − 12/5 = 0.
questions.explanation: A and C are complementary, so tan A = cot C.

questions.text: The point (−3, 5) lies in the ____ quadrant.
Find the distance between the points (1, 2) and (7, 10).

The vertices of a triangle are A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(8, 2).
(a) Find the lengths AB, BC and AC.
(b) Show that △ABC is a right-angled isosceles triangle and name the right angle.
questions.answer:
(a) AB = √[(4 − 1)² + (5 − 1)²] = √(9 + 16) = 5.
BC = √[(8 − 4)² + (2 − 5)²] = √(16 + 9) = 5.
AC = √[(8 − 1)² + (2 − 1)²] = √(49 + 1) = √50 = 5√2.
(b) AB = BC, so the triangle is isosceles. AB² + BC² = 25 + 25 = 50 = AC², so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the angle opposite AC is 90°, i.e. ∠B = 90°.
